That the psalm repeats the fourteenth governs how much anyone is willing to say. Calvin thinks it unnecessary to subjoin any distinct commentary, the two being almost identical, and notes only that the chief difference lies in the fifth verse; whether the variations are owing to transcribers, or were made by some prophetic bard who adapted the older psalm to circumstances it was not composed for, he will not decide — Theodoret held the latter and referred it to the alarm raised by Sennacherib under Hezekiah, while others date it to the captivity on the strength of the closing verse. Clarke says the same and sends the reader back to his notes on the fourteenth, adding only a few short remarks. On the word in the title both are uncertain: Calvin finds it nowhere else and takes it for an instrument, while Clarke reports that some translate it the president, some the leader of the dance, some hollow instruments and some the chorus, and himself prefers a flute — to the chief player on the flute, or the master of the band of pipers.

Augustine reads the title differently and gets the whole psalm out of it. For Maeleth, he says, is found in the interpretations of Hebrew names to mean for one travailing, or in pain; and who travails in this world the faithful acknowledge, since they are themselves that person. Christ travails here, Christ is here in pain, the Head above and the members below — for one neither travailing nor in pain would not say, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? And him with whom, while persecuting, Christ was travailing, he made to travail when converted, since being enlightened and grafted into the very members he had persecuted, and pregnant with the same love, he could say, My little children, of whom I travail again until Christ be formed in you.

What the fool's denial amounts to Spurgeon spells out. He says it because he is a fool, and being a great fool meddles with a great subject and comes to a wild conclusion; the atheist is a fool morally as well as mentally, in the heart as well as the head. With the denial of God for a starting point his progress is rapid, riotous, raving and ruinous, for he who begins at impiety is ready for anything: no God means no law, no order, no restraint to lust, no limit to passion — and what a Bedlam, or rather what an Aceldama, would the world become if such principles were universal. Every natural man, he adds, is more or less a denier of God, practical atheism being the religion of the race. Gill notes the Targum's gloss, that there is no God of whom is revenge, none to punish the wicked.

Henry, having expounded the psalm before, confines himself to three observations about sin. Its fact is proved by an unexceptionable witness, since from the place of his holiness God looks on the children of men and sees how little good is among them, all the sinfulness of their lives lying naked and open before him. Its fault is that it is iniquity, an unrighteous thing in which there is no good, the worst of evils, and what makes this world such an evil world as it is. Its fountain is that there is no fear of God before their eyes, men saying in their hearts that there is no God to call them to account — for bad practices flow from bad principles. Ellicott marks that the conjunction is wanting in the older psalm, and that iniquity replaces the general term doings, as though the adapter felt a word applicable to good as well as evil not strong enough for such profanity; Keil and Delitzsch call the change more bombastic, and note that the later text drops the well-grounded asyndeton of the first.
4:
Most of what is left to say concerns how this text differs from its original. On the word omitted in the fourth verse the three agree and differ only in emphasis: Ellicott notices the loss of the expressive all found in the fourteenth psalm; Clarke reports that seventy-two manuscripts of Kennicott and De Rossi, with several ancient editions and versions, restore it, and adds that where this text has Elohim many manuscripts read Jehovah; Keil and Delitzsch say the word is wanting where it stood in its right place, and describe what the reviser did next. In the older psalm two distichs follow, perhaps each mutilated by the loss of a line, and the writer who retouched this one restored the tristichic symmetry — but by rather violent means, fusing the two distichs into one tristich adapted as closely as possible to the sound of their letters. Gill keeps to the sense, that none of the workers of iniquity lack knowledge, unless given up to judicial blindness.

Over the fifth verse Keil and Delitzsch weigh a theory and reject it. The last two lines are in letters so similar to the two distichs of the older psalm that they look like an attempt to restore a faded manuscript; and though such close following of the sound of letters is found elsewhere — in Jeremiah, and in the relation of the second epistle of Peter to Jude — the two lines sound so complete and full of life that to account for them so takes too low an estimate of them. Rather a later poet, perhaps of the time of Jehoshaphat or Hezekiah, has adapted the Davidic psalm to some catastrophe just then fallen out, giving a special character to what had been a universal announcement of judgment.

The fear where no fear was is the crux, and Ellicott handles it carefully. He calls it the most interesting variation from the older psalm, plainly inserted to suit some circumstance of the time it was adapted for, to which we have no clue. The reading that takes fear in a good sense is excluded, since the same word stands in both clauses; and as it is used elsewhere of a cause of terror, he would render it there were they in great fear, where there was no cause for fear. From the context he judges this said not of Israel's enemies but of Israel itself, and so constantly applicable to a people supposed to live under God's protection yet liable to sudden panics that we need not recover the precise event. Of him that encampeth against thee he renders of thy besiegers, the bones of the beleaguering host lying bleaching on the sand. Clarke reads the added words as levelled at the Babylonians, who sacked Jerusalem and were sacked in their turn; Wesley has God not only breaking their strength but dispersing them beyond hope of restoration, and takes the thee for God's people and the thou for besieged Jerusalem.

At the last verse the two texts coincide again, as Keil and Delitzsch observe, except that the singular salvation becomes plural — the expression strengthened, signifying entire, full and final salvation. Clarke would render the line who shall give from Zion salvation to Israel, notes that many manuscripts keep the singular and that more than twenty read Jehovah where this has God, and sends the reader to Kennicott's Hebrew Bible, where the variations are exhibited at one view. Gill takes the plural the same way, as the complete salvation of the church, and reads the wish forward: what in the older psalm may be a longing for Christ's first coming is here the church's desire for his coming in the latter day, to take to himself his great power and reign, to destroy antichrist and deliver his people, when the Gentiles shall be gathered in and all Israel saved.
